The city employed a man to walk its streets at night and make sure the distances stayed where they belonged.

His name was Emil. He carried a measuring wheel, a thermos of coffee, and a notebook bound in green cloth. Most nights, nothing happened. The distance between the courthouse and the river remained four hundred and twelve meters. The alley behind the bakery continued to be too narrow for a car and just wide enough for a bad decision.

But sometimes a street would stretch.

People assumed this was a trick of fatigue: the walk home feeling longer after a difficult day. Usually it was. Occasionally, though, a block would gain six meters overnight, and someone had to push it back before the morning buses started running.

Emil had worked for the Department of Municipal Consistency for thirty-one years. He was good at it.

His wife had once asked what happened to the extra distance.

“It goes somewhere else,” he said.

“Where?”

“Places people don’t measure.”

She thought about that.

“Is that why the walk to the dentist is so long?”

“That’s a separate department.”

She had laughed with her whole body, tipping backward in her chair. For years after she died, he remembered the laugh without remembering what had caused it. Then one evening, brushing his teeth, he remembered the dentist.

He had to sit on the edge of the bathtub.

***

In November, a small street appeared between a pharmacy and a shop that sold expensive lamps.

There had not previously been room for a street there.

Emil checked his map. He checked the building numbers. He placed one hand against the pharmacy’s brickwork, which was cold and entirely unhelpful.

The new street had seven houses, a chestnut tree, and a yellow light at the far end.

He called his supervisor.

“How long?” she asked.

“Can’t tell from here.”

“Measure it.”

“That seems like encouraging it.”

“Emil.”

“All right.”

He set down his wheel.

At the first house, a woman was sitting on the steps peeling an orange. She wore a blue coat over her nightdress.

“Good evening,” Emil said. “Has this street been here long?”

“For me,” she said.

“Do you have an address?”

“Six.”

“Six what?”

She separated a piece of orange with her thumbnail.

“Would you like some?”

He declined. Municipal rules discouraged accepting gifts from discrepancies.

At the second house, a boy was repairing a bicycle upside down. At the third, someone was practicing the same four notes on a piano.

Emil walked toward the yellow light.

His measuring wheel turned steadily.

After twelve minutes, the light was no closer.

He looked behind him. The pharmacy was still at the mouth of the street, perhaps twenty paces away.

“Oh,” he said.

He had been trained for expanding avenues, misplaced corners, and the occasional staircase that came down somewhere other than where it went up. This was different.

He returned to the woman.

“What is this place?”

She handed him a piece of orange. This time he took it.

“A shortcut,” she said.

“To where?”

“Depends.”

The orange was sharp and sweet. He couldn’t remember the last time he had eaten one outdoors.

***

He came back the following night without the wheel.

The boy was still repairing the bicycle.

“What’s wrong with it?” Emil asked.

“Nothing yet. I’m learning.”

The boy offered him a wrench. Emil held it while the boy took apart the brake assembly, laying each piece carefully on a rag.

“My father used to do that,” Emil said.

“Fix bicycles?”

“Put things in order before he forgot where they went.”

“Did he forget?”

“Sometimes.”

They worked for a while.

At three, Emil’s phone rang.

“Have you classified it?” his supervisor asked.

“Not yet.”

“We need something on the form.”

“Pedestrian.”

There was a silence.

“That isn’t what I meant.”

“I know.”

***

By the end of the week, people had begun to notice.

A nurse came through after a late shift and sat beneath the chestnut tree. A delivery driver leaned his head against its bark. A young couple walked to the yellow light and returned separately, neither looking unhappy.

Nobody took photographs. Their phones stayed in their pockets, as though they had entered a room where someone was sleeping.

The department sent barriers.

Emil stood beside the workers while they unloaded them.

“What’s down there?” one asked.

“An unresolved measurement.”

The worker nodded. He had been employed by the city for eleven years.

They put up the barriers.

By morning, the barriers stood across an ordinary stretch of pavement outside the lamp shop. The street had moved to the other side of the pharmacy.

Emil’s supervisor came to inspect it herself.

“We can’t have infrastructure choosing its own location.”

“No,” Emil said.

“What do you recommend?”

From somewhere down the street came the piano: four notes, a pause, then a fifth.

“Observation.”

“For how long?”

“I couldn’t say.”

***

That winter, Emil began taking his coffee beneath the chestnut tree.

He never found his wife there. He had looked, discreetly at first, then through every window where the curtains were open.

There was the woman with her oranges. The boy eventually rode his bicycle. The person at the piano started a different tune.

Emil still measured the rest of the city. When a road stretched, he put it right.

But each month, on the form for the little street, he wrote: **Still under observation.**

And each month, his supervisor signed it.
